Ishmael son of Nethaniah
ISH-may-el suhn uhv neth-uh-NAHY-uh
noun (proper, assassin)
From Hebrew Yishmael, "God will hear," from shama, to hear, and El, God; son of Nethaniah, "the LORD hath given."

Biblical Definition

Ishmael the son of Nethaniah was a man of the royal seed of Judah who, after the fall of Jerusalem, treacherously murdered Gedaliah the governor whom the king of Babylon had set over the poor remnant left in the land. Gedaliah, son of the godly house of Shaphan, had counseled the people to dwell quietly and serve Babylon, that it might be well with them. Warned that Ishmael came to slay him, Gedaliah would not believe it. So "Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, arose, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him" (Jer 41:2). He slaughtered the Jews and Chaldeans with him, and led away captive the daughters of the king, until Johanan pursued and the people were recovered, though Ishmael himself escaped to the Ammonites. The crime undid the small mercy left to Judah, for the frightened remnant, fearing the wrath of Babylon, fled down into Egypt against the word of the LORD. This dictionary names Ishmael an instrument of treachery whose murder scattered the remnant and drove them into the very land of bondage from which God had once redeemed His people.

Webster 1828 Definition

A man of the royal seed of Judah who treacherously assassinated Gedaliah, the governor set over the remnant after Jerusalem fell. His murder scattered the survivors and drove the frightened remnant down into Egypt against the LORD's word.

ISHMAEL SON OF NETHANIAH, noun. A man of the seed royal of Judah who murdered Gedaliah the governor after the destruction of Jerusalem.

He came under pretense of peace and slew Gedaliah, the Jews, and the Chaldeans who were with him.

"And slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land" (Jer 41:2).

His treachery required no provocation, but proceeded from ambition and the seed royal's envy.

Its sanction was the scattering of the remnant, who fled into Egypt for fear of Babylon.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 25:25 — "But it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, came, and ten men with him, and smote Gedaliah, that he died, and the Jews and the Chaldees that were with him at Mizpah."

Jer 41:2 — "Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land."

Jer 41:10 — "Then Ishmael carried away captive all the residue of the people that were in Mizpah, even the king's daughters, and all the people that remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the Ammonites."

Jer 41:18 — "Because of the Chaldeans: for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor in the land."

Modern Corruption

Ishmael's treachery faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that envy and ambition, dressed as zeal, destroy the very mercy God has left to a humbled people.

expand to see more

Ishmael of the seed royal could not bear that a man of Shaphan's house should govern where he reckoned the crown belonged to him, and so he murdered the governor under the cover of a shared meal. His sin compounded murder with betrayal of hospitality and the wholesale slaughter of the helpless. It is the portrait of ambition that will tear down the little good God has spared rather than submit to His ordering of providence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bitter fruit of treachery against lawful, God-given order. Gedaliah's rule was the small mercy left to Judah, a place to dwell quietly under chastisement; Ishmael's sword destroyed it, and the terrified remnant fled to Egypt, refusing the prophet's word to stay. So one man's envy undid a nation's last refuge, and the people ran back toward the house of bondage. The believer learns to submit to the hand of God in His providence rather than to grasp by blood what He has not given.

Hebrew Roots

His name says God will hear, yet his deed was treachery; the contrast underscores how a covenant name does not sanctify a wicked heart.

expand to see more

Yishmael — "God will hear," from shama, to hear, joined to El, God.

Nethaniah — "the LORD hath given," the name of his father.

He was of the seed royal, a descendant of the house of David, and envied Gedaliah's rule.

He slew Gedaliah at Mizpah under pretense of peace, with ten men of his company.

His treachery drove the remnant in fear down into Egypt, against the word of the LORD.

Usage

"Ishmael son of Nethaniah came under pretense of peace and slew Gedaliah the governor."

"Of the seed royal, Ishmael son of Nethaniah envied the rule given to Shaphan's grandson."

"After Ishmael son of Nethaniah's treachery, the frightened remnant fled into Egypt."
